lines.text: I was fifteen when I finally admitted that I could not swim.
Until then, I had hidden the fact with excuses, so my friends suspected nothing.
Everything changed when my school announces a kayaking camp for the whole level.
lines.note: Tense: the story is in the past, so it is 'announced'.

lines.text: I joined a class at the public pool, ashamed for being the
oldest beginner there. My instructor, a patience woman named Mrs Devi, never laughed.
lines.note: Word form: before 'woman' an adjective is needed — 'patient'.

lines.text: She simply asked me to float. I sank at once, because she made
lines.note: Connector: she carried on in spite of the failure — a contrast, 'but'.

lines.text: me try again. By the third week, I could cross the pool without stop.
What I remember most is not the swimming itself but the relief of
no longer having a secret. At the camp, my confident grew with every stroke.
lines.note: Word form: after 'my' a noun is needed — 'confidence'.

lines.text: Mrs Devi had told me that fear shrinks whenever you faced it.
lines.note: Tense: this is a general truth, so it is 'face'.

lines.text: She was right. I still swim every Saturday, since I no longer need lessons.
lines.note: Connector: swimming on without needing lessons is a contrast, so it is 'although'.

lines.text: Next year, I plan to teach my younger brother myself.
